subject.who: A woman, at Lilly's house in the country
subject.background: Her son was away from home; she did not know where he was staying
subject.question: Is my son with his master, or at my own house?
subject.moment: Question figure discussed as of July 1638 (figure heading in the 1647 printing is partly illegible in OCR: 'Anno Dom. 1638 ... July'); Lilly computed from the ephemeris that the significators of mother and son perfected a trine on 25 July at 2 p.m.

chart_data.asc_ruler: Venus (lady of the ascendant, significator of the querent/mother)
chart_data.key_positions: Jupiter, lord of the 5th (the son's significator), placed in the Ascendant (east angle); Moon in 27° Pisces applying to a sextile of Saturn, lord of the 4th (the mother's dwelling); Mars lord of the 6th in Sagittarius; the absent party also described by Jupiter in the Ascendant and Venus in the 9th
chart_data.note: Positions as stated in Lilly's prose judgment; the full figure is printed as Fig. 3 in the 1852 edition and in Book II of the 1647 original.

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
source.chapter: Book II, the example figure resolving four queries (1st: if a party might be found at home; 4th: if one absent be dead or alive) — 1647 pp.190ff in modern reprint pagination; Fig. 3 in the 1852 Zadkiel edition

subject.background: Asked in the year 1634; Lilly lived to see the outcome ('I have seen the experience of my judgment')
subject.question: (1) Shall I be rich, or subsist of myself without marriage? (2) By what means shall I attain wealth? (3) When? (4) Shall it continue?
subject.moment: 1634, London (exact day not stated in the text)

chart_data.asc_ruler: Venus, lady of the ascendant, near Regulus (Cor Leonis)
chart_data.key_positions: Mars, lord of the 2nd and lord of the Part of Fortune, in the Ascendant near Spica at 18° Libra; Jupiter in his exaltation (Cancer) angular, almost culminating (10th); Moon lady of the 10th in Leo, separating from sextile of Mars and conjunction of Mercury, applying to conjunction of Venus, wanting 6°27' of the conjunction; Part of Fortune in a fixed sign in the terms of Mars; cusp of the 2nd a fixed sign
chart_data.note: Positions as stated in Lilly's prose judgment.

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II

subject.background: In 1634 the inheritance of the house he lived in (in the Strand, London) and others were offered to him for sale; his own money could not be called in for six months; the seller's first demand was £530
subject.question: If I should purchase Master B. his houses — shall I deal with the seller and procure money in time to pay for the purchase?
subject.moment: 31 March 1634, 6 p.m. (figure heading as printed: '31 March 1634. 6 Hor. P.M.')

chart_data.key_positions: Sun (significator of the seller) locally placed in the 7th, received by Venus(?) in exaltation near the cusp of the 7th; lord of the 7th also lord of the 11th (Lilly's hopes); Venus applying to a trine of Saturn, lord of the 4th (the houses); Moon translating light by square aspect out of signs of long ascension; Mercury, lord of Lilly's 2nd, retrograde; Saturn lord of the 4th without material debilities except retrogradation and cadency
chart_data.note: The ascending sign/degree is garbled in the 1647 OCR ('the degree of the Sign is the same wherein [Mars] was in my Radix'); positions above are those Lilly names in prose.

subject.who: A well-affected person (a Parliament sympathiser), asking Lilly
subject.background: 1643, during the Civil War: reports were circulating that the King's forces had taken Cambridge
subject.question: Is the news/report true — has the King taken Cambridge?
subject.moment: 1643 (exact day not stated in the text)

chart_data.key_positions: All angles moveable; Saturn vitiating the cusp of the 10th and Mars the cusp of the 7th (per Lilly's prose); Moon cadent in a sign 'wherein she nothing delights'; Sun on the cusp of the Ascendant; lady of the Ascendant (significatrix of the querent side / Parliament) in her exaltation; lord of the 7th (the King's side) entering his fall and afflicted
chart_data.note: Positions as stated in Lilly's prose judgment.

subject.who: A friend of a London merchant asked on the merchant's behalf
subject.background: December 1644: the merchant had sent a ship to trade to the coast of Spain; repeated news said she was wrecked; insurers refused to insure her at £60 per cent or on any terms
subject.question: What think you of the ship — is she sunk, or living? And afterwards: where is she, on what coast, and when will news come of her?

chart_data.ascendant: Cancer (the ascending degrees of Cancer shew the bulk/body of the ship)
chart_data.key_positions: Saturn in Aries in the 11th casting a square very near the Ascendant; Moon, lady of the Ascendant, in Taurus in the 11th in her exaltation, applying by trine to Sun and Mercury in the 7th (wanting but a few minutes of a perfect trine) and near the body of Jupiter; South Node (Cauda) in the 9th; Part of Fortune disposed of by Mars; Mercury in reception with Mars
chart_data.note: Positions as stated in Lilly's prose judgment.

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II

subject.background: A second example ship figure printed immediately after the December 1644 example; no news had been heard of the ship
subject.question: (Implied, same chapter) What is the state of the ship — lost or safe?

chart_data.key_positions: Moon lately separated from a square of Saturn, lord of the 8th and 9th, then void of course, then applying to a trine of Saturn and afterwards to opposition of Mercury, lord of the 12th and 4th, Mercury being in his detriment and entering combustion; Jupiter, dispositor of Mercury, subterranean and conjunct Mars in the term of an infortune; Mars in his fall near the cusp of the 2nd; Part of Fortune in the 6th, disposed of by retrograde afflicted Jupiter in the 2nd, and in square to both Part of Fortune and Moon; principal significator in the 4th and afflicted
chart_data.note: Positions as stated in Lilly's prose judgment.

subject.who: An unnamed querent asking Lilly during the Civil War
subject.background: Friday 29 March 1644: Sir William Waller's Parliamentarian army and Sir Ralph Hopton's Royalist army were supposed engaged near Alresford, Hampshire (the Battle of Cheriton)
subject.question: Whether Sir William Waller or Sir Ralph Hopton should overcome?
subject.moment: Friday 29 March 1644 (figure erected the day of the engagement)

chart_data.key_positions: Ascendant and Moon, Jupiter and Venus for Waller's side; Saturn lord of the 7th for Hopton; Moon in her exaltation with Jupiter; Sun, lord of Waller's substance/assistants, in the 10th in the very degree of his exaltation (19° Aries); only Mars and the South Node in the 9th (no supplies ready for Hopton); Saturn (Hopton's significator) sub radiis, in his fall, in no aspect to any planet, peregrine, aspecting the cusp of the 7th by square; Moon distant 11° from Venus, swift and increasing in light
chart_data.note: Positions as stated in Lilly's prose judgment (Fig. 20 in the 1852 edition).

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
source.chapter: Book II (Fig. 20 in the 1852 edition): 'A Figure erected to know whether Sir William Waller or Sir Ralph Hopton should overcome'

subject.who: A person of honour asked Lilly
subject.background: Robert, Earl of Essex, Parliament's general, had surrounded Reading with his army; the town was held for the King, governor Sir Arthur Aston (spelled 'Acton' in the 1852 edition)
subject.question: If his Excellency Robert Earl of Essex should take Reading, having then surrounded it with his army?
subject.moment: During the siege of Reading (the town was delivered 27 April; the year is printed '1644' in the 1647 OCR but the historical siege of Reading ended in April 1643 — see notes)

chart_data.key_positions: Mars, lord of Scorpio (the sign ascending per the 1852 judgment), significator of Essex, well fortified except being in his fall, and in reception with the Moon (Mars in her house, she in his terms and face, near Regulus, in the 10th); Moon void of course, applying to a sextile of Mars (equivalent to a square in signs of long ascension); Sun, the King's significator, in the 7th in a fixed sign; Aquarius, the sign on the 4th, for the town; Saturn lord of the 4th for the governor, in his fall; Jupiter lord of the 5th and Venus placed therein for the town's ammunition and provision
chart_data.note: Positions as stated in Lilly's prose judgment (Chap. LXVI in the 1647 printing; Fig. 21 in the 1852 edition).

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
source.chapter: Book II, Chap. LXVI 'If his Excellency Robert Earl of Essex should take Reading' (1647 pp.401–405)
source.version: 1647 first edition (Internet Archive scan OCR); wording cross-checked against the 1852 Zadkiel edition where noted

notes.flag: Outcome year discrepancy: 1647 OCR reads '27th of April, 1644'; the historical Siege of Reading surrendered in April 1643. Treated as a misprint/OCR error and flagged in pending.md — the day (27 April) and sequence (treaties began eight days after the figure was set) are as Lilly states.

subject.who: A London dog owner living at Temple Bar
subject.background: His dog (a small beast, 6th-house signification) had strayed and was missing; London, so Lilly notes he has no example of sheep/hogs to give, only this dog
subject.question: What part of the city should they search? And shall he recover the dog?

chart_data.key_positions: Querent signified by the sign ascending and its lord (Saturn on/near the Ascendant — the querent described as Saturnine); the sign of the 6th and its lord signify the dog; the dog's significator in a western sign, southern quarter verging west; Moon in an airy sign, under the beams of the Sun; Sun and Moon in the 8th; the dog's significator in a sign of the same triplicity as the ascendant (signifying London) applying to a trine of the cusp of the 6th; Sun on the following Monday applying by dexter aspect to Saturn lord of the Ascendant
chart_data.note: Positions as stated in Lilly's prose judgment; several glyphs are garbled in the 1647 OCR.

subject.who: A master whose servant (a young fellow of about nineteen) had run away the Sunday preceding
subject.background: The servant had left his master and his whereabouts were unknown
subject.question: Which way is the fugitive servant gone, and when shall he return / be recovered?
subject.moment: Not stated in the text (servant left on the Sunday before the question)

chart_data.key_positions: Ascendant with its lord and the Moon therein signifying the master; Mercury peculiarly the servant's significator in this figure (the Moon being the common significator of servants); Moon at the time of flight in a western sign and still in the same sign; Mercury in a western sign, south quarter; Moon in the 2nd in her own house; Sun in the 2nd in perfect aspect with a planet in the 11th; servant's significator and lord of the Ascendant hastening to a trine out of angles
chart_data.note: Positions as stated in Lilly's prose judgment.

subject.who: A lady who had long been courted by a gentleman suitor; she had continually slighted him and finally given him an absolute denial, then bitterly repented and wished the match revived
subject.background: She came to Lilly in great heaviness, asking whether the match could be brought on again without scandal to her honour; Lilly first read her own history from the figure, which she then confessed in full
subject.question: Can this marriage match be revived/effected?
subject.moment: June of an unstated year (Lilly advised the gentleman to make the first move on 19 June near noon; Saturn and Mars came to aspect on 27 June)

chart_data.key_positions: Sun, lord of the Ascendant, significator of the lady; Saturn, lord of the 7th, significator of the gentleman, in the south angle in conjunction with Mars in a fixed earthy sign, elevated; Moon separated from [the gentleman's significator] void of course, applying to opposition of the Sun; reception between Venus and the Moon, and between the Sun and Venus; Moon disposing of Saturn in her exaltation; Jupiter in his exaltation applying to a sextile of Saturn, lord of the 7th, and transferring Saturn's virtue to the Sun, lord of the Ascendant, with no prohibition, abscission or frustration before the aspect perfected (perfected 27 June)
chart_data.note: Positions as stated in Lilly's prose judgment.

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II

subject.who: A clergyman (the querent, described by Lilly as covetous, of good wit and volubility of tongue) seeking a benefice
subject.background: He had lately lost the benefit of some good place in the Commonwealth and was solicitous how to live in his former credit; he pressed his suit for the parsonage despite Lilly's advice
subject.question: If he should obtain the parsonage (benefice) desired?

chart_data.key_positions: Saturn impedited in the Ascendant, 'infortuning' the question; Jupiter lord of the 9th (significator of the benefice) in no aspect with Mars(?) lord of the Ascendant, nor the Moon in any aspect with him; neither lord of the Ascendant nor Moon placed in the 9th; no translation or collection of light, and no reception between the significators; Moon separating from a trine and applying to an opposition of Mercury, lord of the 3rd; Venus in the 7th house opposing the Ascendant
chart_data.note: Some planet glyphs are garbled in the 1647 OCR; the seven numbered negative testimonies are Lilly's own enumeration.

subject.who: William Lilly himself, living in the country (Walton-on-Thames)
subject.background: He had bought fish in London for his Lenten provision; it came by barge to Walton, and on Saturday 10 February 1637 (Old Style) a waterman told him their warehouse had been robbed the night before and his fish stolen; Lilly erected the figure for the exact time he first heard the report
subject.question: What became of my goods — who stole them, where are they, and can I recover them?
subject.moment: Saturday 10 February 1637 (Old Style; 1637/8), at the moment Lilly first heard the report

chart_data.key_positions: Jupiter, the only peregrine planet in an angle, on the cusp of the 7th, in Scorpio (a moist sign) — taken as significator of the thief; Mercury, significator of Lilly's goods, in Pisces (a moist sign); Part of Fortune in Cancer (a moist sign); Moon in Taurus, an earthy sign, under the earth; Mercury, lord of the 2nd, in his fall and detriment but in his own terms, applied to by sextile of the Moon (lady of the Part of Fortune) and having a trine to the Part of Fortune; Mars lord of the 7th leaving Scorpio, his own sign
chart_data.note: Positions as stated in Lilly's prose judgment (Fig. 19 in the 1852 edition).

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
source.chapter: Book II, theft chapters — 'Explanation of the above Figure' (the stolen fish), Fig. 19 in the 1852 edition
source.version: 1647 first edition (Internet Archive scan OCR); wording cross-checked against the 1852 Zadkiel edition where noted

subject.who: A querent whose money had been stolen; he suspected a woman servant (shown by Mars) and another (shown by Saturn) and tried to persuade Lilly of it
subject.background: Question of theft: who is the thief, and shall the money be recovered?
subject.question: Who stole my money, and shall I have it again?

chart_data.key_positions: Mars, lord of the Ascendant, in 25°02' Leo, in square to Mercury and Saturn, but in his own terms and face (therefore refused as the thief's significator); Saturn in the west angle (7th, house of theft) likewise in his own term and face (also passed by); Mercury in an angle, having no essential dignity, in partile conjunction with Saturn and square to Mars — taken to signify the thief; Moon in a masculine sign applying to Mars; Mercury conjunct Saturn and square Mars, both masculine planets; Moon so near the Sun, separating
chart_data.note: Positions as stated in Lilly's prose judgment (Fig. 18 in the 1852 edition).

subject.who: A gentlewoman whose husband was at sea; she was herself extremely disfigured by smallpox, weak-eyed, full of grief for her husband, and chronically ill (Saturn, lord of her 6th, retrograde — she relapsed from one disease into another)
subject.background: She asked Lilly about her absent husband; Lilly judged both the husband's state and, from the same figure, her own fate
subject.question: A woman asked of her husband at sea: if alive, where, and when shall he return?
subject.moment: Not stated in the text (the death Lilly timed from the figure fell on 8 October following)

chart_data.key_positions: The 7th house taken as the woman's ascendant in this question; Saturn lord of the 6th retrograde; the husband's significator (the Sun, per Lilly's prose) in her hayz and free from all affliction; Mars and Saturn moving to an ill aspect, Mars then near the place of the Moon in the question (about 2° of a sign) and Saturn in about 2° of Capricorn, the Moon at that (later) moment in about 20°
chart_data.note: Positions partly garbled in the 1647 OCR; the husband's significator being wholly unafflicted and the timing of the wife's death are the two points Lilly states unambiguously.
